summary: This component detects phone shake gestures by monitoring accelerometer data and displays a fun Easter egg—a scared meerkat image—when a shake is detected. It uses a 'jerk' calculation (how quickly acceleration changes) to filter out normal jitter, includes a cooldown period to prevent repeated triggers, and manages the overlay's visibility with fade-in and fade-out animations.

explanations.10: This is the sensitivity threshold for detecting a shake; it's measured in units of acceleration change per second. The comments show it was tuned over time because initial values fired too easily from just tilting the phone.
explanations.14: The device motion sensor fires very frequently on some phones (60+ times per second), so we ignore samples that come in faster than every 100ms to avoid treating tiny natural jitter as a shake.
explanations.30: We store the previous acceleration reading so we can calculate how much the acceleration changed since the last sample—that rate of change is what we check against the shake threshold.
explanations.36: This helper function cancels any pending timeouts so we can clean up old timers before starting new animation phases.
explanations.55: The optional chaining operator (`?.`) safely calls the vibrate function only if the browser supports it; many browsers require a user gesture first, so this just silently does nothing if not allowed.
explanations.66: We check if we're in a server-side rendering environment (where `window` doesn't exist) and if the browser supports the motion sensor API before setting up the listener.
explanations.74: The accelerometer data might have null values for any axis, so we need to explicitly check all three are actual numbers before we try math on them.
explanations.84: We skip this sample if it came in too soon after the last one; this filters out the high-frequency noise that would make every tiny wobble look like a spike.
explanations.90: Jerk is the rate at which acceleration is changing, calculated as the sum of changes across all three axes divided by time. We multiply by 1000 to convert from per-millisecond to per-second.
explanations.97: We only trigger the Easter egg if the jerk exceeds our threshold AND enough time has passed since the last trigger, so one shake gesture doesn't fire the overlay multiple times.
explanations.111: This cleanup effect runs on unmount to clear any remaining timers, preventing memory leaks or timeouts firing after the component is gone.
